extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, philosophers of science, and advanced students/researchers interested in mathematical explanation
extracted.subtask_description: Survey and analysis of proposed criteria and models for when a mathematical proof counts as explanatory, comparing externalist (ontic) and internalist (epistemic) approaches and reporting various positive and negative tests against mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bottom-up taxonomy of explanatory proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by avoiding commitment to a particular theoretical framework, collect a rich and varied set of examples, and attempt to provide a taxonomy of recurrent types of mathematical explanatory proofs to see whether patterns are heterogeneous or can be subsumed under a general account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocated by Hafner & Mancosu, Mancosu, Lange and others; emphasizes diverse case studies across mathematical areas and resists a single general pattern — at most different classes of explanatory proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity (Lange)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a proof of a simple result, the proof should 'exploit some similar, simple feature of the setup.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lange treats simplicity as a salient feature that in some contexts distinguishes explanatory from non-explanatory proofs (see Lange 2017, 257).

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry (Lange)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a theorem displays striking symmetry, an explanatory proof must show how that symmetry follows from a corresponding symmetry in the problem's setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: d'Alembert's theorem: explanatory proofs should reveal that symmetry arises from invariance of complex arithmetic under substitution of i for -i. Note criticisms that what is isolated as 'symmetry' may instead be an appropriate structural feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-dependence of explanatory status
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction between explanatory and non-explanatory proofs is context-dependent rather than absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resnik and Kushner (1987) argue for context-dependence; several bottom-up approaches stress examining proofs within their specific mathematical/practical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steiner's characterizing-properties account
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof explains when one deduces the behavior of an entity from its essence or nature, more cautiously phrased as deducing from a 'characterizing property' unique to the entity or structure within a family.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steiner rejects other candidate criteria (abstractness, generality, visualizability) and adds that explanatory proofs should be generalizable: varying the relevant feature should yield an array of corresponding theorems proved by 'deformations' of the original proof. Criticisms: problems with 'essence' and counterexamples (Resnik & Kushner; Hafner & Mancosu).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstractness, generality, visualizability (considered and rejected by Steiner)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstractness, generality, and visualizability were considered as potential markers of explanatory proofs but were ultimately rejected by Steiner as adequate characterizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned as possible criteria but Steiner found them insufficient to capture explanation in mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weber & Verhoeven's deformation/pairwise-explanation criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatory relation can be analyzed by comparing pairs of proofs: P1 explains why class x has property Q by using a characterizing property of x, while P2 explains why class y has property Q' by using a characterizing property of y; both use the same axioms and rules but differ in which characterizing property they exploit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focuses on when pairs of proofs count as explanatory and refines Steiner's idea of deformation by starting from relations between proofs rather than single-proof essences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterfactual account (CF1/CF2)
rubrics_metrics.description: F explains G iff CF1 is true and CF2 is false: CF1 — 'if F had not been the case, G would not have been the case' must hold; CF2 — 'if G had not been the case, F would not have been the case' must be false (ensuring asymmetry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires a truth-conditional semantics for counterfactuals. Two main implementations: (i) possible-worlds semantics (with extensions to avoid trivialization for mathematical counterfactuals); (ii) structural-equations/causal-model framework (treating mathematical facts as variables and testing by intervention). Critics argue about meaningful variation of mathematical facts and abundance of true countermathematicals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible-worlds and impossible-worlds semantics for countermathematicals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use closeness-based possible-worlds semantics extended to include impossible worlds to evaluate mathematical counterfactuals needed in the counterfactual account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lewis-style semantics trivializes for mathematics; extensions (Nolan, Priest) allow evaluation of CF1/CF2 for mathematical explanations. Used by Reutlinger et al. and Baron et al.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural-equation modelling / intervention test (counterfactual via Pearl)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model mathematical facts as variables (exogenous/endogenous); test CF1 by intervening on the variable for F to see if it changes the variable for G — interventions reveal dependence relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gijsbers adapts structural-equation methods but replaces interventions with 'quasi-interventions' because causal interventions don't straightforwardly apply to mathematics; Frans & Weber propose a mechanistic model generalizing Woodward's interventionist ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasi-interventionist approach (Gijsbers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce 'quasi-interventions' that reveal asymmetries inherent in mathematical practice rather than objective features of proofs; explanatory asymmetries are tied to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifts explanatory asymmetry from an objective property of proofs to features of mathematical practice; complementary to mechanistic accounts that attempt to model interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanistic/interventionist model (Frans & Weber)
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for explanatory power of proofs using a mechanistic model of explanation that generalizes Woodward's notion of intervention to the mathematical context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aims to capture explanatory relations by identifying components/operations in proofs whose variation affects results, modeled analogously to mechanisms in empirical sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract-entity-invocation criterion (Pincock)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is explanatory when it invokes more abstract kinds of entities than the topic of the theorem it proves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires formalization of proofs in logical systems for precise assessment; similar proposals by Wilhelm and Poggiolesi use formalization to assess explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity–depth balance in formalization (Wilhelm)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a formalized proof, explanatory power arises from a balance between the simplicity and the depth of the formalized proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilhelm assesses explanatory power in terms of formal proof characteristics (simplicity vs depth) after formalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase of conceptual complexity in formalized proofs (Poggiolesi)
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanatory proof (in its formalized version) is distinguished by an increase of conceptual complexity from the assumptions to the theorem it establishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poggiolesi's proposal relies on formalization to detect conceptual-complexity gradients that signal explanatory proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kitcher's unificationist criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanations provide understanding by unifying different phenomena: the best systematization minimizes the number of argument patterns used while maximizing the number of conclusions generated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formally, the explanatory store E(K) is judged by three factors — (i) the number of patterns, (ii) the stringency of the patterns, and (iii) the set of consequences derivable. Kitcher's model aims at global unification across a body of knowledge rather than local proof-by-proof distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical adequacy with mathematical practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed theory of explanatory proofs should make predictions that align with judgments from mathematical practice; mismatch counts against the theory's adequacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hafner & Mancosu show Kitcher's model makes predictions about explanatory power that contradict mathematical practice; thus empirical fit to practice is an evaluative standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding-centered functional account (Inglis & Mejía‑Ramos / Wilkenfeld)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define explanations as those things that generate understanding; explanatory proofs are those that produce understanding according to functional criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using Wilkenfeld's functional model and Kelp's conception of understanding, Inglis & Mejía‑Ramos identify three properties likely present in explanatory mathematical proofs: (i) they direct the reader's attention to the conceptually important section; (ii) they reorganize new and existing information into coherent new schema; (iii) they reduce the chances of exceeding working-memory capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style-related and related-virtue connections (beauty, purity, depth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatory arguments relate to mathematical style and virtues such as beauty, purity of method, and depth; these aesthetic and methodological virtues inform judgments about explanatory status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connections drawn in literature (Giaquinto, Lange, Detlefsen & Arana, Skow, Ryan) suggest explanatory value can be tied to notions of purity, aesthetic appeal, and depth in proofs; these function as background evaluative criteria rather than a single formal test.
